historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors

starting.description: The program developed from a biological relationship between testosterone, DHT, the 5-alpha-reductase enzyme, and androgen-dependent tissues, with human inherited enzyme deficiency later accelerating the work. The investigators' subsequent clinical rationale included the small prostates observed in adults with inherited deficiency.

inspiration.description: Endocrine conversion of testosterone to DHT and clinical studies of inherited 5-alpha-reductase deficiency supplied the biological rationale. The 1986 chemistry article summarizes an additional clinical prostate observation from an earlier report.

steps.description: A Merck BPH project drew on androgen biology and recognition of the testosterone-to-DHT conversion.
Human enzyme-deficiency reports accelerated the work and were followed by a decision to screen for inhibitors.

Earlier steroid screening found enzyme inhibition in vitro but not in intact animals; a search for less readily reduced inhibitors produced active 4-azasteroids, followed by structure–activity investigation.

Rasmusson and Reynolds synthesized the inhibitor MK-906, which was selected for development and later marketed as finasteride. The exact date of its synthesis relative to the 1986 report is not established here.

A 1986 paper documented additional structure–activity studies using human and rat prostatic enzyme and rat androgen-receptor assays to identify potent, selective inhibitors; its publication date does not establish when MK-906 was synthesized.

design.description: Researchers deliberately screened steroid compounds, sought agents less susceptible to reductive metabolism, synthesized azasteroid derivatives, varied A-ring and C-17 structures while measuring enzyme and receptor activity, and synthesized MK-906; the underlying biological relationship preceded this design work.

circumstances.description: Merck's screening for a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor was planned; the original clinical observations are a separate stage.

limits: The founding history is established for the Merck finasteride program represented by the supplied cohort, not independently for every later inhibitor.

S5 describes the later dual-isoenzyme inhibitor dutasteride, which is outside the supplied cohort; its independent founding history and any distinct starting clue were not reconstructed. This later difference in activity is not by itself evidence for a separate design-from-scratch founding branch.
conflicts: Chronology and scope: S5 says Merck began a development program after the deficiency findings became known; S1 describes earlier androgen/BPH interest and a late-1960s biological insight, followed by a post-1974 decision to screen. These accounts may refer to different program stages; no pre-1974 internal records were examined to resolve the precise chronology (E1, E2, E9).
Isoenzyme wording: S5's Main Points says finasteride inhibits type 1 only, whereas its body and Table 3 say type 2. This internal inconsistency does not determine the class-origin judgment (E10).
gaps: The 1974 original was read only as an abstract; its full article has not been read. The 1986 chemistry paper summarizes the small-prostate finding with a citation to a 1976 clinical review whose full text was not read.

The exact compound-by-compound transition from early azasteroid leads to MK-906 and exact synthesis date relative to the 1986 article have not been reconstructed; the discoverer retrospective attributes MK-906 synthesis and later finasteride development.
Pre-1974 Merck internal records and the original Walsh–Wilson clinical report were not read; a later dual-inhibitor program was not traced independently.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: The phenotype of inherited 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, including small prostates, strengthened and accelerated inhibitor development.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: Merck work was already underway; the human finding was not the sole initiating event and laboratory screening was extensive.

relatedReading.title: Depression risk of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors: impact of active-comparator versus non-drug user control groups on risk measurement
relatedReading.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies
relatedReading.whyRead: Examines how depression associations differ when 5-ARI users are compared with non-drug users or alpha-blocker users.
methodologicalQuestions: Do comparison groups have similar indications, disease burden and opportunities for depression diagnosis?
How much heterogeneity remains within each comparator group?
Could residual confounding affect either direction of association?
relatedReading.interpretationLimit: Comparator-sensitive observational findings do not by themselves establish causation or the absence of adverse effects. Check the population and indication before applying a finding to a different group.

relatedReading.title: Risk of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in New Users of 5-Alpha Reductase Inhibitors: A Nationwide Historical Cohort Study
relatedReading.design: Nationwide new-user observational cohort in South Korea, using tamsulosin as the active comparator
relatedReading.whyRead: Investigates incident diabetes among people treated for benign prostatic hyperplasia, using weighting to balance measured baseline risk factors.
methodologicalQuestions: Which confounders were measured, balanced by weighting or left unmeasured?
How do eligibility, lag periods and treatment discontinuation or switching affect follow-up?
Does the target population have the same indication and baseline diabetes status?
relatedReading.interpretationLimit: The comparisons concern incident diabetes in the studied BPH population. Weighting addresses measured confounders, and the study does not establish equivalent risks or eliminate residual confounding.

relatedReading.title: Risk of poor glycemic control in tamsulosin versus finasteride users with type 2 diabetes mellitus
relatedReading.design: Population-based observational cohort in New Zealand comparing tamsulosin and finasteride users with existing type 2 diabetes
relatedReading.whyRead: Addresses glycemic control in people who already have diabetes, a different outcome and population from incident-diabetes research.
methodologicalQuestions: Which medicine is the reference group for the reported effect estimate?
How was poor glycemic control defined and measured?
What range of effects remains compatible with the confidence interval?
relatedReading.interpretationLimit: Interpret the estimate and its uncertainty together. An imprecise or non-significant comparison does not establish equivalence or an absence of effect.
